speechtext:
As my hon. friend and the house know, yesterday Israeli armed forces carried out attacks into Jordanian territory. These Israeli forces, I understand, have now been or are being withdrawn. There seem to have been losses in men and equipment on both sides. As my hon. friend undoubtedly knows, the Security Council has been meeting since yesterday afternoon to consider the situation, and it is our hope that the council will be able to take action to bring about not only a restoration of the cease fire but a more effective observance of the cease fire in the future. I understand that resolutions are being considered now informally pending a meeting of the Security Council later this day.

March 22, 1968

continued sabotage activities in Israel. The government, and I am sure the house, deplore the acts of violence that have taken place between the two countries which, in addition to inflicting needless suffering on the local population, have prejudiced and made more difficult the task of the United Nations special representative, Mr. Gunnar Jarring, who is trying to assist the parties to attain a just and lasting settlement in the area.
We hope, and I know the house hopes, that both sides will exercise moderation and restraint and avoid steps that can only impede the establishment of peace. Mr. Speaker, in recent days the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria has asked a number of questions concerning the manpower situation at the North Sydney terminal of the C.N.R. ferry service to Newfoundland. The changes in the ferry service were announced in 1965. It was then


estimated that they will result in the displacement of between 500 to 700 longshoremen at North Sydney.
The government has therefore decided to assess the situation through its manpower consultative service program. To date several hundred men were counselled as to the possibilities of alternative employment. Some 150 men have received or are receiving intensive retraining, close to 80 men accepted alternative employment with the C.N.R.., and another 100 found employment elsewhere.
Our efforts under this consultative arrangement with the company and the union are, of course, continuing. Our manpower officers are on the spot and doing their utmost to assist the affected men. In some cases the solution is not easy. The company has made more than 1,000 offers of employment but the men are reluctant to leave the immediate area. The consultative committee has retained the services of motivation specialists in trying to overcome these difficulties.

30c. To provide for the insurance, on a shared risk basis with the lender, in the current and subsequent fiscal years, up to an aggregate amount of $100,000,000 on such terms and conditions including the payment of such fees therefor as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council, of loans made before January 1, 1973, under the Adjustment Assistance Program related to the Kennedy round agreements, by private lenders approved by a board established under section 15 of the Department of Industry Act to manufacturers in Canada who, in the opinion of the said board,

Mr. Chairman, not long ago when he was in opposition, I believe the Prime Minister was one of those who objected violently to the implementation of statutory legislation by means of estimates. As I understand it we have not passed the adjustment assistance program and in fact have not completed any discussion of the Kennedy round in the legislative sense in respect of what our liability would be and what displacement would take place. Yet we are being asked by means of this statutory item to implement a program about which we have not had any previous knowledge.
I was particularly interested in the minister's reply when he said this supplementary estimate is related to another item of $10 million which appears in the projected estimates with which we are not yet concerned. Therefore I wonder why the Prime Minister has agreed to the implementation of this legislative process by estimates. Personally I am opposed to statutory items except on an emergency basis. If this is an emergency I should hope the minister would give the committee a much fuller report than he has given concerning what might be the implications. Without knowing what displacement is taking place because of the Kennedy round tariff agreement we now are being asked, I presume, to compensate companies which already have gone through the process of establishing what their losses may be and which have gone through the process of appeal to the financial institutions which would be in a position to make loans available to them.
As I read paragraph (a) we are now being asked to underwrite or provide for a loan in a situation where a loan would not otherwise be available. I presume this is similar to the situation in respect of programs where after a company has made application to two banks and has been turned down, a loan can be made through the fund. Since this item is asking for $1 obviously it is not really asking for the establishment of a fund but rather is asking for a statutory authority. Therefore I think these items should be noted very carefully. Certainly this is not the proper way to pass legislation. I believe the Prime Minister was one of those when in opposition who

were very much opposed to statutory items, because this would mean that parliament would not be allowed any opportunity to examine the legislation.
I can only guess, because it is not so stated, that if we pass this item we will be passing in some measure the adjustment assistance program. Personally I am of the opinion that this is not the way it should be passed. I believe we should have the full discussion which was promised in respect of the implications of the Kennedy round. This type of item is not one which allows the full discussion which I believe should take place.

In so far as the interest rates are concerned, they will be normal commercial rates. I think the hon. gentleman understands that the role of the government of Canada in this program is to act as insurer of loans which the banking community might feel, in light of their normal policy, involve too great a risk. To remove some of this risk the government will act as insurer with

No dollar limit has been set on the loan or the amount to be insured. The borrower will be charged a premium for the insurance, and it is expected that over the course of this program the premiums on the insurance will cover any losses that might be required to be made good under the insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the hon. gentleman says "Let us have a little more candour" I would point out that a standing committee of the house has examined at considerable length the Kennedy round, its implications, the proposals under the general heading of the adjustment assistance program and the steps proposed by the government to deal with the program. The steps proposed involve a number of actions by more than one department comprising a program of the government. It is quite an extensive program.
Some of the elements of the program require legislative authority. In so far as my department is concerned there are two elements requiring legislative authority; one, the launching of an insured loans program to make available financial means to those who wish and are able to take advantage of the opportunities offered by the Kennedy round. We anticipate that another element will be required at a later date, although not nearly as early in the chain of events as the insured loans scheme; indeed, the insured loans scheme should be in operation now. That is why it is in the supplementary estimates.
[DOT] (12 noon)
The second element of the program is for a different purpose and a different set of circumstances, and that is the reason for the change in wording of the vote in the main estimates to which the hon. gentleman has just referred. It is designed to deal with hardship rather than the exploitation of opportunity. It is not expected that these cases of hardship will develop to the point where they can be adequately dealt with at an earlier date, and consequently the provision in the main estimates will meet the time frame.
In addition to that-and this was pointed out at the time as part of the problem of dealing with the change brought about by the Kennedy round-the Minister of Labour, in a different act and at a different time, has sought and obtained the approval of the house to the scaling upward of the unemployment insurance benefits. This is part of the program also, as was outlined to the committee. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will not wish me to recite again in the house the detailed exposition which was given before the committee at a series of 22 meetings.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I was present at every meeting of the

committee and I can say that no details were given to us at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get into a debate with the hon. gentleman, but I wonder what the committee which produced a report on the implications of the Kennedy round meant to do and what in fact it did in 22 meetings.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like the minister, I do not want to have to spin this out but I do think that in legislative terms this is a rather serious matter. As a result of our exchange this morning we have already dicovered that in addition to item 30c in the present supplementary estimates there is item L95 on page 597 of the estimate for next year.
I have been doing some further checking and I find that on page 257 of the estimates for next year there is another item under the Department of Industry for $1 million for grants to manufacturers in Canada who have applied for government insured or direct loans under the adjustment assistance program. Thus there are three different items in the estimates of this department, one in the present supplementary estimates and two in next year's main estimates, all referring to the adjustment assistance program. I think it is significant that in all cases the first letters of the words "adjustment assistance program" are printed in capital letters. This is a program of substance, not just one of words.
The minister says that the changes in the unemployment insurance rates and benefits were part of this program. I recollect quite well that when the government made its announcement about what it was going to do as a result of the Kennedy round it said it was going to work on two fronts. It was going to do something for industry and something for workers. May I point out to the minister that in the case of unemployment insurance benefits, in the case of what was done for workers, a regular statute was passed by the house amending the Unemployment Insurance Act. Nothing was said in that legislation to the effect that it was part of some nebulous adjustment assistance program. It stood on its own feet. This makes me believe that the adjustment assistance program is mainly under the purview of the Minister of Industry, although I gather from the discussions which may or may not have taken place in the committee that it does not yet exist in legislative terms. But once we have passed this item containing the words "adjustment assistance program" in capital letters we will
.March 22, 1968

have enacted it. Perhaps this is a good thing and the house wants to do it this way, but I still think that legislating in this way by these $1 items is a questionable procedure except in ad hoc emergencies or in special cases. I think under some conditions, perhaps involving a retired civil servant's pension, it might be appropriate, but a major program of adjustment assistance should be on a legislative par with the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I am not examining the substance of the issue but, if I may go back to the phrase I used, I think this is a shoehorning method of getting on to the statute books something which until now is not there. There is no adjustment assistance program of legal effect on the statute books of Canada as of now. When we pass this $1 item and the estimate becomes part of the supplementary estimates and a supply bill is passed, then it becomes statutory and we will have the adjustment assistance program which may lead to a lot of things. Perhaps it is desirable, but I think the least the minister could do is to admit he is getting this piece of legislation through in the easiest possible way.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister does not want to mislead hon. members when he says the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs went into the full details of the adjustment assistance program. What actually happened was that prior to the first meeting the Prime Minister issued a statement setting forth the areas in which assistance would be given, and some of the witnesses before the committee were deliberately evasive with regard to the details. I am not complaining about that because they probably had not worked out the details at that time. However, the minister is not correct when he says that the committee went into it in detail. I do not think the minister's officials had worked out the details at that time.
I recall that three areas were discussed. The first was government insured loans, the second was direct loans, and the third was consultative services. Mr. Chairman, regardless of the observations of the minister concerning the discussion of the details of this item I think he would not deny that vote 30c has an important aspect to it. The minister may or may not recall that there have been occasions in the house when the whole question of one dollar legislative items has been the subject of considerable discussion. In my view the question has never been properly resolved. It is a matter of continuing concern to many members in addition to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that this method of legislating appears with increasing frequency. It may have merit. However, there appears to be an increasing tendency to carry through significant and important legislative measures by means of one dollar items in the supplementary estimates. Sometimes these items go through with little or no examination in the committee. If we are going to follow this practice, then ministers should pay particular attention to trying to make sure that these proposals fit into some orderly legislative framework by giving a detailed statement in the vote. In this case, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has pointed out, approval of this item will mean-I am not discussing the desirability or otherwise of the program-we will bring into being a capitalized adjustment assistance program.
As it happens, I have a copy of the Department of Industry Act with me because of some discussion we had on another matter yesterday. Section 15 of that act clearly states:
The governor in council may establish advisory and other committees to advise or aid the minister or to perform such duties and exercise such powers as the governor in council may specify, and may fix the remuneration and expenses to be paid to the persons so appointed.
I wonder whether the minister would be prepared to consider some clarification of the wording of vote 30c which would perhaps help to clarify the existing legislative authority from which the proposal in this vote flows?

I have been looking at the act and section 7 reads in part:
The minister shall-
(c) develop and carry out such programs and projects as may be appropriate
(i) to assist the adaptation of manufacturing industries to changing conditions on domestic and export markets, and to changes in the techniques of production,
I may be wrong in my assessment but it would appear to me there is some flow of authority from section 7 of the Department of Industry Act with regard to this one dollar item. To that extent I assume the minister would be prepared to argue that he has acted within the scope of his authority in bringing forward this proposal. I am not quarrelling with him on that score. However, it does seem to me it would be much easier to have an understanding of what we are doing if there were a clear reference to the basic parliamentary statute from which this authority flows. If my assessment is correct, I wonder whether the minister might be prepared to consider an amendment to the wording of vote 30c somewhat to this effect: "To provide, as provided in section 7 of the Department of Industry Act." In this way there would be a ready reference which would enable anyone concerned with this measure to understand what we were doing when in effect we pass a bill without going through first, second or third reading stages. Would the minister indicate his reaction to what I sincerely feel is a helpful suggestion under the circumstances?

All the hon. gentleman is doing here is documenting the statutory authority of the Minister of Industry to engage in this particular activity. Mr. Chairman, as I say I am
not in favour of this item. The minister is passing judgment on the assistance program and I have heard my colleagues say that they do not know what the terms of this program are. When the house approved of those benefits I am sure the minister did not say that as a result of the Kennedy round tariff negotiations the workers of the country would be required to increase their contributions to the fund. No department is more qualified than the minister's department to establish a new program. Supply-Industry
item we are entitled to discuss the matter as we would discuss any piece of legislation introduced into this house.
If I remember correctly, when the area development assistance program was passed it was preceded by a piece of legislation. There is no doubt that the minister has authority to establish programs under the act. However, the act does not provide for establishment of such programs by interdepartmental action; they must be established by legislative action on the part of this house. My objection is to legislative action being taken by means of a statutory item of one dollar when we are unfamiliar with the details of the program.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out that if an important person died without provision being made for a pension for his widow, a statutory item could be introduced for that purpose. I am sure everyone would agree, even the members of another party who are not at all interested in estimates, that problems of particular individuals cannot be considered even though we admit there may be an oversight in a specific case. However, payments may be made out of the general revenue fund provided a one dollar item is passed.
This adjustment assistance plan is going to involve a great deal of money in many fields and I am sure will be in existence for some time. Situations will change; indeed, things have changed since the initial discussions took place on the Kennedy round. For this reason alone the minister should not only be willing to introduce this item in some other manner but should welcome the opportunity to do so.
The minister mentioned three programs, one of which was in relation to unemployment insurance. I am sure he agrees this is not the most important program of the three. Although there may be difficulties, these can be overcome in another way. I have always maintained that there are some smart people in the ministers' department, and the discussion this morning is an indication that this is not a facetious observation. speechtext: But it was referred to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as my hon. friend knows, as a consequence of the agreements achieved at Geneva in respect of lowering tariffs around the world a considerable
March 22. 1968

number of export opportunities have been presented to Canadians through the lowering of the tariffs of other countries. In order for Canadian manufacturers and processors to take advantage of these opportunities, changes in their previous modus operandi have to be made. If they are to seize the opportunity they must change what they have been doing in type, kind, skill or volume. Generally speaking this has required some physical changes, and physical changes normally require financing.
The object of the Department of Industry is to provide all the assistance it can to enable Canadian manufacturers and processors to take advantage of these increased opportunities. This particular item is related to the process of taking advantage of opportunities. In the case of those who for one reason or another, either because they are high risk borrowers under normal commercial arrangements or because they have an inadequate corporate financial structure, are unable to secure commercial loans to take advantage of opportunities, then the department under this arrangement, if in the opinion of the board which is mentioned here the changes are economically sound and viable and are directed toward taking advantage of the opportunity, will undertake to provide on behalf of the government insurance with a commercial lender. We are prepared to make loan insurance available to cover the added risk of this kind of loan.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
The hon. gentleman has asked me whether Sysco would be eligible for assistance under this provision. That would depend on the plans Sysco may have to take advantage of the increased export opportunities offered by the Kennedy round. Whether Sysco has any such plans I confess I do not know. If the company does have such plans involving additional financing and if it is unable through its own normal commercial financing to carry out these changes, then this section will come into operation.

Supply-Industry
The minister mentioned the benefits which will be derived from the Kennedy round. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
I do not have the detailed information as to tariff changes in connection with steel, though this can be obtained. I believe the hon. gentleman is fully aware that in tariff terms the duty on steel is a complicated affair. There is no such thing as just "steel". The word covers a great many categories, a great many forms, and as a consequence there are a great many specialized tariff arrangements. I confess I do not pretend to carry in my head all these classifications and all the changes which have been made, but if these are of interest to the hon. gentleman I will see that the information is provided.
So far as benefits to the steelmakers of Canada are concerned I can only point out that there has been a reduction in the tariff affecting the import by foreigners of steel produced in Canada. This does, of course, provide more opportunity for those who are interested in exporting steel, and some of our producers have been very successful in this field. I admit there is a counterpart to this benefit, namely, a lowering of the barriers against the inflow of steel into Canada, which permits increased competition domestically. But in the case of steel the tariff changes have perhaps not been too significant because the tariffs on most forms of steel have, in international terms, been relatively low, not an item of major significance. Of more significance are the provisions relating to dumping. But that is another story unrelated to the point we have been considering and it will be the object of legislation to be introduced at a later date. It has formed the subject of an exhaustive examination by the committee on finance and trade.

speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. Of necessity I must be repetitious because what I say now I shall repeat when the minister returns to the house. It is regrettable that the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, when making inquiries of the minister this morning, did not receive the co-operation of the house. When the Minister of Manpower and Immigration asked for permission to revert to motions in order to make a statement with regard to the very serious aspects of the employment situation in

Cape Breton he was not permitted to do so because the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough rejected the request that a statement be made. The only choice left open to the minister at that time was to ask for supplementary questions.
Now that the Minister of Industry has returned to the house I should like for a few moments to refer to a remark he made when questioned about the Kennedy round. The minister referred to dumping. It is a well known fact that any nation in the world which is making progress must have a basic steel industry. In Canada the basic steel industry is very badly affected because of the fact that cheap steel is imported. I realize that quite often this is referred to as dumping, but it is dumping only if the imported steel which is undermining the basic Canadian steel industry comes into Canada at a price cheaper than the cost of production in the country of origin. I realize that if the request I am about to make were granted there might be repercussions on the international scene. However, since steel is so basic to the Canadian economy perhaps the minister would consider consulting with his colleagues about the possibility of bringing about a change in the definition of dumping.
I believe the government should take steps to redefine the meaning of dumping if this could be done to the advantage of Canada. Although we understand it is not dumping as long as the product is landed in this country at a price which is not below the production cost in the country of origin, nevertheless there is a great difference in this case between the landed price and the Canadian production cost. Therefore I ask the minister and his colleagues to review the situation so that possibly the definition of dumping could be related to the Canadian production cost rather than the production cost in the country of origin. In this way I believe a great deal of the disparity in prices could be eliminated to the advantage of the Canadian steel industry. If it would appear that the advantages would be greater than the disadvantages, then I think the government should take a hard look at the situation and bring in a redefinition of the term "dumping".
With reference to the Sydney steel industry the minister apparently is not aware of the representations which have been made with regard to this matter by some of his own colleagues. In respect of the negotiations between the federal and provincial governments he said earlier that further developments were taking place. But after he had
March 22. 1968

resumed his seat someone whispered in his ear and he jumped to his feet again. At that time he said that there were no further developments. Either the minister or whoever whispered in his ear is not up to date in respect of the situation which prevails now with regard to the negotiations between the federal and provincial governments. If they are, then what the Prime Minister said in the house the other day was not completely in accordance with the facts.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
When answering that question directly the Prime Minister said-the minister looks at me now with some interest-that he was awaiting a reply from Premier Smith on the latest correspondence which had been forwarded to him. So for the minister to stand up one moment and say there are developments, and then to immediately deny it, is further evidence of the fact that attention is not being paid to the negotiations going on between the federal and provincial governments respecting the Sydney steel industry. This should shame the minister who professes to have an interest in and to be concerned about the problem in Sydney.
I also remind the minister that one of his colleagues, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, told an audience of 20,000 people in Sydney that the federal government was searching desperately for a way which would assist in bringing about a satisfactory solution of the problem faced by the Sydney steel industry. "Searching desperately" were the words used by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
This is no longer a Cape Breton problem; it has become a Nova Scotia problem because all the people of Nova Scotia are assisting in this regard. The taxpayers of Nova Scotia are carrying the load. The government of Nova Scotia put a very simple solution before the federal government. The government of Nova Scotia asked that the federal government lend them 50 per cent of the purchase price of this plant. The federal government took the callous attitude that this assistance would not be made available, which is a complete denial of the Minister of National Health and Welfare who said that his government was searching desperately for a way in which to assist the industry. The federal government has a simple out, namely, to lend the government of Nova Scotia 50 per cent of the funds necessary to purchase this plant.
How desperately has this government been searching for ways in which to solve this
Supply-Industry
problem? How honest has it been in its promise to assist the Sydney steelworkers? On Monday of this week the Prime Minister, in a nationally televised program, said that if it was a matter of spending money to keep men employed he would be happy to spend that money.
The province of Nova Scotia has asked for a loan of about $12 million for this purpose but the federal government has callously refused to make that loan. At the time this appeal was before the government the Minister of Trade and Commerce signed an agreement to lend $20 million to the government of India. What I have said in this regard has been interpreted as a stand on my part against foreign aid. This is not the case at all. The fact that I object to the government lending a foreign country $20 million, while it refuses to lend a provincial government a little better than 50 per cent of that amount, is another indication that this government is not at all concerned about the problem and is not supporting the statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare who, I repeat, said that the federal government was searching desperately for a way in which to help the steel industry of Sydney. Hon. members opposite like to interpret the stand I have taken in this respect as one that is against foreign aid. They like to say I am against feeding the starving children of India. This is the inference that has been drawn respecting my objection to $20 million being lent to India while a loan of $12 million is refused to a province of Canada in order to assist Canadian citizens.
I think that in the long run the federal government would benefit from such a loan being made to the province of Nova Scotia. If the government lent that money to Nova Scotia, in the next few years it would be collecting income tax on the wages earned by Sydney steelworkers. If the government continues its callous attitude, 3,000 Canadian citizens will be out of work, and not only will the government not collect income tax on the wages that would have been earned but it will be compelled to pay unemployment insurance to these people. This represents a considerable amount of money.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that a government which professes to be searching desperately for a way in which to help these people has lent a foreign government $20 million while refusing Canadian citizens the opportunity to go to work. I say this is a complete denial of
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
I would simply like to ask the hon. member whether he could tell us from whose mouth came the refusal by the federal government to extend this loan.

It is
rather difficult to pin it down to individuals because the government has a spokesman, and in this case the spokesman appears to be the Prime Minister. I can truthfully say that at no time did the Prime Minister say there was an absolute refusal, but I do not think there is too much question about the attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is a Nova Scotian. He stated outside the house that this plant is not an economic unit and should therefore go down the drain. As I have pointed out, in refusing this help the government is denying Canadian citizens, its Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. speechtext: This is an important department and we have been waiting for some time to discuss these estimates. I wonder whether the minister would make a report on the activities of his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know exactly how to tackle this subject, so varied is the work of my department.
My department is indeed very active in numerous fields. As everyone knows, it comprises four large branches. The first is the geosciences division which conducts all types of research, from geology to astronomy.
The second is the mineral development division which is concerned mostly with mining economy and the administration of certain mining statutes relating, for instance, to gold and the continental shelf.
The third is the water division which has developed the most rapidly in the past year. I shall say a few words a little later about the water policy.
The fourth division is that of energy, which has started to develop and is headed by an assistant deputy minister. It will soon include a number of advisers in matters relating to hydro-electric energy, coal, uranium, gas and oil.
These are the main sectors.
The hon. member would perhaps like me to talk more specifically now about our water policy. This past year, we have developed a policy based on certain basic principles. We are often asked in the house: When will the government state its policy concerning water resources? I have the impression that some members think that a water policy is developed much in the same way as instant coffee is produced. That is not the case. There already exists a water policy at the federal level. It needs to be improved, which is what we are doing. However, the difficulties in this case should not be underestimated.
Everyone knows that water has many uses. It is used for shipping, for the production of energy. It is the natural habitat of small fish. It is also used in homes, industry, farming, etc. That is the multifunctional aspect of water.
Everyone knows also that there are conflicts between users. Some of them come to mind easily: conflicts between the interests of hydro-electric developments and those of shipping, conflicts between the recreational and the economic objectives.
March 22, 1968

In that field, as in some others, there are also conflicts of jurisdiction. I do not wish to repeat the speech I have made so many times to the effect that, in some cases, water comes under provincial jurisdiction and in others under federal jurisdiction.
I have outlined that situation many times. We have, in Canada, a federal system which has tremendous advantages but which presents some difficulties. I have often said that the water problems could be approached only in a multijurisdictional or comprehensive way, which implies a close co-operation between federal and provincial governments.
These principles which I have outlined very briefly will be found in the legislation which we hope to present during the next session, and we hope that parliament will accept it.
In the meantime, I must say that, in the best spirit of co-operative federalism, we have had conversations with the provinces last year at the administrative and political levels, directly and during meetings of the resource ministers council.
On the other hand, at the very time when new legislation is in the mill, my colleagues should not think that the minister and his department are inactive. On the contrary.

I might say a few words on the question of water supply. For years the department has been making an inventory of the water resources of Canada and we have special agreements with some provinces in this respect. May I mention two of them. We have an agreement with Ontario concerning the investigation of water supplies of northern Ontario rivers. We have been working on that for two years now. A few months ago we reached an agreement with the three prairie provinces on the creation of the Saskatche-wan-Nelson River Board. This is an extremely important move, because, as hon. members realize, we will be taking in Canada more and more a basin by basin or region by region approach to water problems. I feel this should be an element of comfort to everyone who is interested in this problem.
In the field of flood control, which comes under the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act, we have already spent $8 million and another $14 million is committed mostly for projects in Ontario and British Columbia. More important still, the Winnipeg floodway is coming to completion. The federal government has already spent $33 million on the 27053-501
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources construction of this great work. As I said this morning, we are about to enter into a most important water flood control project, the Fraser one. I see some of my hon. friends opposite nodding in satisfaction. Such an agreement has been talked about for a long time following the 1948 flood which caused extensive damage. Now, Mr. Chairman, after the accumulation of a tremendous number of documents dealing with the subject, we are finally coming to an agreement with British Columbia on this matter.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I do not want to spend too much time on it at the moment as I am sure there will be occasion to talk about it later, as everybody easily realizes the value of this project. The Fraser is an extremely important river in the economy of British Columbia and of the other western provinces. The federal government has a clear responsibility here not only in terms of flood control but in terms of navigation, fisheries, transportation and the prevention of national disasters. Therefore my department and I feel that this agreement will be a great accomplishment. In the first ten years both governments will share in an expenditure of some $30 million as was already paid last summer when agreement in principle was reached.
I will also be asked, so I might as well answer now, about what steps we are taking against pollution. This is a favourite subject of some of my hon. friends on the other side. Following the Montreal pollution conference my department made an analysis of the conclusions that were reached there. We then formulated a number of recommendations which we brought to the attention of the provincial ministers, this area being one of shared jurisdiction, as is well known. I brought these matters to the attention of my provincial colleagues at the Montreal meeting of the council of resource ministers last May and asked for their comments. These have been coming in. I do not have to tell hon. members that they are not all in agreement with the views of the federal government; as hon. members know, these subjects are debatable.

speechtext: Are they all in agreement with each other?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, obviously not, and that is an added difficulty. I should not like to leave the impression that we are simply sitting around waiting; that would be
March 22, 1968
7980	COMMONS
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources wrong. One of the most important developments in this field is the decision to build at Burlington, near Hamilton, a Canadian inland water centre. Some $17 million will be spent on the construction of this centre. It is to be built at Burlington, on the Great Lakes, for very good reason: the main interest of the federal government in pollution matters has to do with pollution of the Great Lakes.
I think everyone will agree that this should be so. Obviously the federal government cannot be made responsible for depolluting every little creek in the country. This would normally be the responsibility of the municipalities and the provinces. However, the federal government does have clear responsibility for and jurisdiction over the Great Lakes. These are international waters and international waters fall mainly under the authority of the federal government. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think it is a good idea to concentrate much of our financial, capacities and personnel in this Great Lakes area. The universities and provinces will be admitted of course to work with us on research leading to depollution of the waters of the Great Lakes. All of the work done at Burlington will be communicated across the country, even across the world.
There are already 80 people from my department located there. Temporary buildings are already built on pier 19, I think it is, and we will be acquiring land in the coming days. So things are moving ahead. My estimates have been cut on a number of occasions, as have the estimates of other departments in recent days-only a little more, I feel-but we have protected this project because it seems to us to be the most important measure the department can take in the coming months and years.
I might add that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is continuing to lend money for the construction of sewage treatment plants. The last time I checked, about $225 million had been allocated for that purpose. Again this is a very important contribution by the federal government in the field of inti-pollution control.
A few months ago, as my hon. friends remember, the provision in the income tax regulations allowing rapid depreciation of industrial anti-pollution equipment was extended in force until 1970, which again is a great contribution to anti-pollution. It is only in so far as there is an incentive in terms of tax deduction that the provinces can assume their full responsibilities in this field and


through moral suasion, persuasion or governmental pressure bring industry to recognize its own responsibility to instal anti-pollution equipment in their new plants.
I could go on but I think I will stop at this point and give members of the committee an opportunity to question me more specifically.

I was interested in the minister's remarks a few moments ago about a water supply inventory. I wonder whether the people of this country realize how much water we need.
March 22, 1968

The Ontario government recently issued a little pamphlet which gives some indication of how much water we need for our various activities. I read this paragraph from that pamphlet:
Up to 62,000 gallons of water are required in the manufacture of one ton of newsprint; 750 gallons to process one barrel of oil; 25 to 200 gallons for one case of cannery products.
That clearly shows what the water requirements of this country are, and I hope to see the minister active in seeing that an inventory of our water supply is taken. I hope he will make certain that the water needs of this country are met before commitments with respect to water are made to other countries.
I wish to ask two or three questions. Looking back through Hansard I saw that on June 14, 1967, when the house was in committee of supply and dealing with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the minister had this to say, as found on page 1518:
At this point I should like to say a few words about each of the main sectors of my department, namely mines and geosciences, mineral development, water and energy. First of all, in respect of mines and geosciences, the principle objective of this sector is to keep up a high level of survey and research in mineral and geosciences so we can learn better the nation's potential mineral resources.
This raises an important point because I now want to speak about the survey of our mineral potential. I agree with my colleague from Timmins who said yesterday that our mineral resources have been barely tapped. We have almost unlimited mineral resources.
I do not quarrel with that statement but we must look at the matter from the point of view of communities which have been built around mineral resources in any given area. Both I and the hon. member for Sudbury are concerned about resources that can still be mined in the Sudbury area.
Has the minister worked in co-operation with mining companies such as International Nickel at Falconbridge to ascertain to what extent ore bodies have been staked out in our area and for how long in the future it is expected that these ore bodies can be worked? I know that Falconbridge and International Nickel have been expanding their operations in the Sudbury area, as they have been doing at Thompson, Manitoba. I want to know if these operations are being expanded in an orderly and normal fashion. Is thought being given to managing these resources so that the affected communities will be kept viable not just for one or two generations but 27053-5011

Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources for many generations to come. That is an important consideration. If mining companies are permitted to mine out all of an ore body in a given area where communities are solidly established, it will be only a matter of time, perhaps not more than 10, 20 or 50 years, before those communities face serious economic difficulties. All this must be ironed out between the minister's department and the mining concerns involved. I wish to know if the minister has any control over this situation.
Too often in the past we have seen what has happened to worked-out areas. Hundreds of families have been dislocated and many hardships have followed that dislocation. Elliot Lake is a prime example. I have been saddened to see houses boarded up in Elliot Lake, to see houses ruined by burst water pipes because they have not been heated in winter. I have seen houses in a sad state of disrepair, verging on ruin. What effect that has on our total economy is hard to assess, but we must avoid this sort of thing in other mining localities.
Of course, there is a partial answer to what ought to happen to mining localities after an ore body has been mined out. The matter does not come under the minister's jurisdiction, I agree, since it involves secondary industry. Judging from the success we have had in establishing secondary industries in the Sudbury area, our best bet is to retain the mining companies for as long as possible.
Though it has been said we have unlimited natural resources in this country, I must say that sometimes I am sceptical. Not too many years ago we were told we had unlimited supplies of timber. Consequently I was amazed to see in the Globe and Mail yesterday a report that the chief forester of MacMillan Bloedel Limited, one of the largest timber operators on the west coast and perhaps in Canada, had said that within 20 or 30 years we shall face an extreme timber shortage. I say that we ought to be concerned about conserving our resources and our mining resources in particular. We ought to develop our mineral resources in an orderly way so that ultimately we do not create ghost towns with their dislocated families and so on. If the minister's department has not taken positive action in this field, it ought to do so.
I was interested to hear that the department is to be involved in Arctic exploration. This is a move in the right direction. In view of the fact that many of our oil fields are not producing at their potential capacity and that we

The minister said something about air pollution. As I recall, he tied it in with water pollution. But I should like to remind the minister that where there is air pollution soil pollution and water pollution follow. In the area from which I come air pollution has killed trees and vegetation for miles around. The soil was poisoned and this poisoned soil wound up in our streams with the result that our streams too are polluted. The city of Sudbury faced a serious pollution problem two years ago when the city water was not fit to drink. I am sure the cause of this water pollution was originally the pollution of the air. It cost the taxpayers of Sudbury a great deal of money because the water had to be treated. I am not sure whether it is still being treated. I know it had to be treated for some months, and even if it has not been necessary to continue treatment during the winter I believe treatment measures will have to be resumed again this spring.
There is one aspect of water pollution with which the federal government is directly concerned. Some time ago I spoke on the ten o'clock show about the water pollution in the Elliot Lake and Bancroft areas. I referred particularly to conditions in the Elliot Lake area because I had visited that area myself and seen what was happening at first hand. I based my short speech at that time on a report known as the report on radiological water pollution in the Elliot Lake and Bancroft areas, presented, I understand, by a deputy ministers' committee of the provincial government. One of the statements made in that report is as follows:
It now appears that provincial statutes are inoperative in view of the overriding authority assigned to federal agencies under the Atomic Energy Control Act.
I may be wrong but I believe the responsibility for the administration of that act comes within the duties of the minister. Recently I received a complaint from an individual with respect to what is happening at a new uranium mine opened between Sudbury and the Elliot Lake area. I had firmly intended to visit this area myself and perhaps to make a report to the minister, but as yet I have not had an opportunity to do so. The man who wrote to me said that nothing had been done to dam an effluent from this mine which was flowing directly into a creek known as John


creek which in turn flows into Agnew lake. I understand that this is one of the best fishing grounds in the region. I have only this gentleman's word for what is happening but I believe I can rely on it. I hope to go there myself in the next two or three days to see what the situation is and I shall certainly bring this matter to the minister's attention if what is asserted is correct.
Let me say at this point that when I was making a tour of the Elliot Lake area I was told that Quirke lake, which not many years ago was one of the best fishing spots in that region, no longer held fish because of carelessness in damming effluents from various mining operations. I also heard that the Serpent river and its tributaries, as well as the lakes through which they flow, are almost devoid of fish. This is a serious situation and it concerns an aspect of pollution which closely involves the department.
I have the impression that arrangements for inspection in connection with this kind of pollution are very poor. Indeed, I believe on some authority that this is the case. I have visited a number of mine properties and it was evident that in many cases only a halfhearted effort had been made to do something about disposing of the waste from mining operations. In fact it is pointed out in the report to which I have referred that in some cases intervention was necessary to ensure that proper damming was carried out. In other cases no action was taken simply because the mines had been closed. We should bear in mind, however, the possibility that many of these mines will be re-opened. The effect of this type of pollution on an individual exposed to it is still obscure. This is another aspect which was brought out in the report to which I have referred. the plants and gardens where he lives. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words about a subject the minister touched on which is of particular significance to many people in British Columbia. It is the long awaited and extremely important Fraser river flood control project. I wish to do two things briefly. One is to give some praise and credit to the minister for what I know he has done to bring agreement with British Columbia nearer to completion. The other is to encourage his colleagues, or those of them who may be present this afternoon, to support him in concluding the agreement.
As the minister has said, this project involves many millions of dollars. The idea for the project goes back about 15 or 20 years. I hope that with co-operation between the federal government and the British Columbian government we shall actually see the agreement put into effect this year and flood control on a comprehensive basis begin in the lower mainland of British Columbia. I use the words "lower mainland of British Columbia" because it is through that area that the Fraser river flows and it is in that area that all too often flooding has taken its toll.
In British Columbia there are approximately 2 million people. Half of them live and work on less than one half of one per cent of the land area of the province, which in round terms encompasses the lower mainland of British Columbia. When the Fraser river running through that area, through the municipalities of Langley, Surrey and Delta and past the city of New Westminster, floods, the economic consequences to the people, the
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources farmlands and the industries in the area run into millions of dollars.
There are two types of floods to which the area is subjected. One is winter flooding which particularly effects the municipalities of Langley and Surrey. The ground level flooding resulting from water coming down from the higher areas of the valley, the much less diked area of the valley, covers thousands of acres. I have seen photographs taken in the 1920's, 30's, 40's and 50's showing the effect of this flooding. Recently I saw photographs taken only a month ago showing its effect. Every winter thousands of acres are under water as a result of faulty drainage and lack of flood control in that part of the valley.
The other type of flood is the more spectacular one which threatens almost every spring. Hon. members may recall that last spring people in British Columbia felt that flooding was imminent and that it might result in a major disaster such as they had experienced in previous years. However, as it turned out there was no major flood. But there is no guarantee that there will not be one in any given year. This type of flood results from the melting snow in the upper areas coming into the river with the result that it overflows its banks. The economic losses from both types of floods can run into large sums of money, affecting a great number of people.
Many industries are concerned about the flood problem. The only regret I have is that this comprehensive co-ordinated plan among the federal, provincial and municipal administrations to grapple with the flood problem has taken so many years to come to fruition. Mr. Chairman, at the same time perhaps I might reply to the previous speakers. I do not have much to say in answer to my friend the hon. member for New Westminster because his address was mostly informational and complimentary. I should like to pass the compliments on to my officials, as I believe every good minister should. I should also like to pay a compliment to Mr. Willis-ton, the minister of lands, forests and water resources of the province of British Columbia. Often it is said that there are difficulties in federal-provincial relations. It is not often said that there also is a tremendous amount of good co-operation at the political and official level. Unfortunately what appears in the news reports is information concerning the clashes, while what does not appear in the headlines is the tremendous amount of cooperation that exists. This is regrettable, and I thought this would be a good opportunity to make the observation.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt made three main points. The first had to do with information in respect of mineral resources. I do not wish to labour the problem with regard to jurisdictional divisions because he is just as much aware of this as I am. The hon. member is also aware that the federal jurisdiction in respect of mining is a limited one. Besides scientific research and the administration of a few mineral acts, the officials of my department are mainly involved in the preparation of economic analysis for trade purposes, internal and international.
I think it is well known in Canada that we have in the department of Energy, Mines and Resources one of the best groups of mineral development analysts. For example, numerous articles describing the situation with regard to these resources and the trade possibilities are published every year by the department. While reading mineral magazines I sometimes have the impression-of course exagerated-that most of the writers in that field are members of my department. They are doing an extremely worthwhile job in keeping the industry and the public informed of the situation in the industry. Some of these articles appear under my name. It is obvious that I do not write them. They emanate from my department, and that is the reason why they are so good.
The information which is used is obtained from D.B.S. reports, annual reports of companies, correspondence with the companies, and
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources in some instances from visits, inquiries and investigations. As my hon. friend knows there are a number of assistance programs administered by the department, for example the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. In carrying out their duties in these cases the officials of the department do more than merely inquire; they go around and visit the mines in order to obtain the information they require for the proper administration of the laws.
Another point raised by the hon. member had to do with pollution in the Elliot Lake area, as a result I believe of the nuclear energy development. As he said, this comes under the jurisdiction of the Atomic Energy Control Board, which has limited personnel. For the purpose of carrying out its investigations this board wherever possible uses the existing facilities of the provincial health departments. I am quite sure my hon. friend would not like the Atomic Energy Control Board to double up on the services offered by the provinces. I have followed the development of the previous cases in which there has been federal-provincial co-operation. However, I am not familiar with the specific case the hon. member now raises. I will inform myself on this and be in touch with him in that regard.
On the question of pollution in general, and air pollution in particular in respect of which the hon. member placed a good deal of emphasis, may I say it sometimes seems that my hon. friends regard me as being the minister responsible for all water pollution, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare as being the minister responsible for all air pollution in our country. To a degree I am passing the buck, because my department has a responsibility over resources in general. I agree with the hon. member that sooner or later the federal and provincial governments must take an over-all approach to the problem of pollution-air, water and land. This will have to be done because there is an obvious inter-relationship between the different types of pollution.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has stated that he is interested in presenting a "clean air" bill, and this, I am told is being prepared. In addition, as is well known a "water bill" administered by my department, will be introduced soon in the house. I believe we should proceed with what is most urgent, according to all the experts who have freely expressed opinions on this
March 22, 1968

Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources subject. They all believe that the most urgent aspect of the pollution problem is that which pertains to water. Then we could proceed to bring together the other aspects of pollution in what might be an environmental bill.
It is not necessary for me to remind my hon. friend that we are in a situation which involves a divided, shared, or overlapping jurisdiction. This is frequently ignored by members of the New Democratic party. I listened yesterday to one member who suggested that we should not be bothered by constitutional difficulties. That is easy to say but dangerous to do.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I believe all my hon. friends, especially those who sit opposite, but far to my right, will agree that the federal system is the only one under which this country can live politically. If one is to have that system of government, then its disadvantages as well as its advantages must be recognized. If we had had a unitary form of government in Canada we would have had also many troubles of course different from the ones we have now. It is vital that we recognize that we have divided jurisdiction in water matters, that the federal government has some responsibilities and that the provinces have some also. Having recognized this, we have to add immediately that unless the two levels of government get together, hardly anything will be done, because each level of government has the ability of preventing the other level from acting. This is what I have been repeating all along-and I think it is correct-that divided jurisdiction in this country is not un pis aller, as we say in French, or a second best; it is the only way to go, there is no other way to act under our federal system.
This is the mystique, if I may be lyrical for a few seconds, that has to be created, namely that there has to be federal-provincial cooperation because it is the only way to do things in this country in many areas of government activities, if not in most. Unless we are adult enough, mature enough to understand that, we will create all kinds of unnecessary troubles and will slow down our economic and political development.
Again I repeat that in the field of pollution the main responsibility is with the provinces. Hen. members may very well come back to me and say that air has a tendency to move from one province to another, and they may show me a map which illustrates that water has a tendency to move from one province to


another and both air and water seem to ignore the constitutional system, but that does not change the fact that we have in Canada a divided jurisdiction in water matters.
While I am very willing to accept some of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Nickel Belt, I should also like to remind him that some of his friends in Toronto, and some of mine in Quebec city, should exercise pressure where it should be exercised in the first place. I am almost fanatical, if one can be fanatical about something of this kind, in building up with the provinces the policies of co-ordination which are very necessary in the whole field of resources development. Again may I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that this is the only way in which we can accomplish important things.

I agree with the minister that there is a division of responsibility in this field. I should like to say a word or two about the mapping service. This is an area in which I believe Canada is a long distance ahead of most other countries in the world. We have the longest shore line in the world and probably the largest uninhabited territory in the world. The mapping facilities we have been able to develop in Canada are second to none. The reproduction machinery we use for map compilation is probably as good as has been developed. I understand that many countries are interested in the technology we have been able to develop in this field.
Perhaps this is an area the minister could consider when we are talking about assistance to foreign countries. Since many Canadians are reluctant to make a general contribution in the form of external aid but are willing to provide technical assistance, and since one of the problems of these countries is their inability to develop a mapping service to make surveys of the potential of their countries, I was wondering if the minister would give some consideration to making some of our people available to these countries. This would enable them to

Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources take advantage of the techniques we have developed to a very high degree.
The last point I should like to mention, Mr. Chairman, is the roads to resources program. I should like to ask the minister to extend this program this year. I have said that the work being done in remote areas by the federal government and by provincial governments in this field has been very extensive. When I look back at the history of northern Ontario, I am always impressed to find that when the initial survey crews went through northern Ontario before the turn of the cen-try, about 1886, they made an assessment of the potential of northern Ontario in resource materials.
It is interesting to note that during that short period of time, probably not more than two years, the ten crews surveyed the whole potential of northern Ontario. They made a catalogue of the many resources of the area. Since that time both the federal department of mines and the provincial authorities have completed the catalogue. It is interesting to note that this survey of northern Ontario not only pinpointed where the mines were going to be, but where townships were going to be developed that would be suitable for cultivation. This is surprising when you recall that these areas were all covered with timber at the time. The townships indicated on the survey are almost identical with the farming areas and townships that exist today. The mineral areas were pointed out long before silver was found at Cobalt or gold at Kirkland Lake.
This roads to resources program is not the haphazard development it may seem. When we agree to a roads to resources project, we are not taking a chance on the development of some resource as a result of the implementation of that project. We are fairly sure, as a result of the outline that has been given by the geologists and other members of the mines branch. The letter in question was from a Mr. William R. Warnick, a professional engineer of R.R. 2, Lowbanks, Ontario, and in it he talks about the fertilizer plant near Dunnville, Ontario, which received wide publicity as a result of a C.B.C. program to do with fluoride pollution. The minister mentioned a possible amendment to the Income Tax Act under which industry would be allowed a tax write-off in connection with money spent on pollution control equipment. It is debatable whether this would be a good policy because its application would mean we were asking the people of Canada to make a donation to enable industry to instal anti-pollution equipment, and I do not think this is a fair charge against the public.
I believe the cost of installing anti-pollution equipment is a fair charge against the profits of the company developing the resources. If those resources are worthy of being developed, then all the expenditure properly involved in their development should be borne by whomever is making a profit out of the operation, not by the rest of Canada. I do not see why Canadian citizens should have to subsidize profit making corporations in an area such as this.
In some countries a method of weighing pollution and imposing taxes accordingly has been adopted-the reverse of what has been suggested in this committee. As I pointed out, there is one plant which is dumping 4.8 tons of fluoride into lake Erie every eight hours. Why should we not levy a penalty of so much a ton in respect of the pollution which this plant sees fit to pour into the Great Lakes? The penalty could be $100 or $200 a ton, I do not care how much. But as the pollution is reduced, so would the penalty be reduced.
I understand that an incentive system of this type is in use in one of the most heavily industrialized areas of the world, namely the Ruhr valley. The money collected is used by the government to instal further anti-pollution equipment. In the long run the cost of this equipment is provided by industries contributing to pollution. I would point out that usually the pollution is in direct proportion to the profits a company makes, because if it is not considered necessary to install anti-pollution equipment, profit rises. This is why it is hard to persuade industry to spend money upon equipment which is regarded, in some cases, as non-productive. So instead of the taxpayer having to contribute to the cost
Supply-Energy, Mines and Resources of anti-pollution equipment I suggest a penalty tax imposed on a tonnage basis as an incentive to companies to clear up pollution, in order to rid themselves of extra taxation.

subtopic: PERMANENT STATUS FOLLOWING RECOVERY FROM MENTAL DISORDER
PERMANENT STATUS FOLLOWING RECOVERY FROM MENTAL DISORDER
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-30, to amend the Immigration Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this proposed amendment is to give permanent status under the Immigration Act to immigrants who have suffered from a mental disease or disorder but who apparently have been cured. Persons who have been convicted of and imprisoned for crimes are granted permanent status after a period during which they have demonstrated their rehabilitation. Under the present provision of the act persons who have ever suffered a mental illness are not given a like opportunity to prove their recovery.
In the white paper on immigration the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) has in fact recognized the sheer discrimination contained in the present regulations by indicating the government's general intention. At page 24, paragraph 58, the white paper contains the following statement:
Scientific knowledge and medical skill have reduced substantially the element of risk once inherent in certain illnesses. The present grounds for prohibition do not altogether reflect this advance. Nor are they altogether in line with modern medical and sociological concepts, particularly in respect to mental illness and epilepsy. Persons actually insane or suffering from contagious or infectious diseases ought not to be admitted as immigrants or non-immigrants, unless they are coming to Canada by previous arrangement and under proper safeguards to take treatment. However, an illness that has been cured or brought under control, to the point where no danger to public health or safety exists, should not be a bar to either temporary or permanent admission. Nor should mental or physical defectives be excluded for that reason alone, but only if they represent a danger to society or are not assured of private care.
I am now very pleased to report, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has indicated to me that he approves the general intent of this bill. He agrees with me that one of the most urgent needs for change in the Immigration Act is the removal of that section which authorizes the minister to issue a deportation order on a legally entered immigrant if the said immigrant should have the misfortune to enter a mental home.
At present, under the Immigration Act, a landed immigrant who has the misfortune to be admitted to a mental hospital is immediately placed under deportation order, and this order is not removed after the patient has
March 22, 1968

been discharged from hospital fully recovered, even though he may enjoy many years of good health and never suffer a relapse.
This is a total disregard of justice, for even though the unfortunate individual has completely recovered from his mental illness he cannot recover his status as a landed immigrant. Although he may live an honourable life, reaching old age, he cannot qualify for citizenship because the act as it stands does not give the minister the power to remove the deportation order.
The fact that a deportation order is never acted upon in instances such as this does not alter the fact of this outmoded legislation, which is the worst encroachment on the rights of individuals ever to be put on the statute books of Canada. For many years I have viewed with alarm the retention of the present provisions of section 5 of the Immigration Act dealing with insanity, and I am thankful that we have been promised the removal of these provisions. Immigrants who have suffered from a mental disorder and who have been discharged as cured from a mental hospital, if all other qualifications required under the Citizenship Act are met, should not be denied Canadian citizenship.
I know of cases of persons right now who are unable to qualify for Canadian citizenship because of this monstrous section in the Immigration Act. These unfortunate individuals, with families, directing their own businesses, even employers of labour, suffered a nervous breakdown and had to undergo treatment in an Ontario mental institution for a period of months, but they were later discharged as cured and they have never suffered a recurrence of the disease.
Until this legislation is amended not only is such a person unable to qualify for Canadian citizenship but he cannot leave the country, say, to visit his homeland, which is a perfectly normal desire, for if he were to do so he would find himself in the prohibited class of persons who could never re-enter the country.
Now, sir, I wish to give you some of the details of a case in my own constituency. Without requiring lengthy consideration, any reasonable person would come to the conclusion that here was a case of unparalleled inconsistency in government legislation. In 1954 an order of deportation was issued against a man in my constituency, whose name for obvious reasons I shall not divulge; but the facts are all too true. Two and a half years after his arrival in Canada from Italy he was confined in the Ontario Hospital at Port Arthur for a
Immigration Act
period of two months, following a nervous breakdown. After his discharge from hospital he continued to work for various companies, including the Canada Car Company of Fort William, until 1957, when he accepted a position with the Marathon Corporation of Canada. Then in 1961 he started a business of his own, which he still operates, employing three other persons. At about this time he applied for Canadian citizenship, but was of course rejected.
When the present government took office in April, 1963, this fellow appealed to me for help to obtain his Canadian citizenship. Although I received a sympathetic response from the department, my representations on his behalf met with no more success than his previous attempts. Nevertheless I kept at it in the hope that surely there would be a breakthrough in this unjust regulation, and today I am pleased to say that this breakthrough has occurred, or is about to occur.
I personally appealed to the then deputy minister of citizenship and immigration, and on March 26, 1964, I received a reply from which I wish to quote in part as follows:
I have reviewed the immigration branch file concerning your constituent, which indicates that he was granted landed immigrant status in May, 1951. He was getting along satisfactorily but unfortunately, in August, 1953, he became ill and was committed to the Ontario Hospital at Fort William. He was discharged after a short time but within a matter of days was returned to the hospital where he remained for over a year.
Full particulars of the case were referred to the immigration medical advisers who diagnosed his condition as "schizophrenia catatonic type". An immigration inquiry was held and in February, 1954, his deportation was ordered on the grounds that he had become an inmate of a hospital for mental diseases. Although his appeal was dismissed, as he had been discharged from the hospital and had resumed his employment, deportation proceedings were deferred indefinitely.

Over the years, this individual has called periodically at the immigration office in Fort William, in an effort to have his landed immigrant status restored. Unfortunately, his history of mental illness places him within the categories of persons whose admission to Canada is prohibited by statute. Under the present Immigration Act there is no provision for removing him from the prohibited classes and unless legislation is passed to change this situation no action can be taken towards his landing.
No unfavourable reports have been received concerning this individual and you may assure him that in his present circumstances he may be allowed to remain in this country indefinitely under deferred deportation proceedings. You might also wish to advise him that the immigration officials will review this matter from time to time and that if any change occurs which would allow for
