Immigration Act
restoration of his status, his case will he considered.
In view of your interest I am sorry that my reply is not more encouraging. Yours sincerely.
On March 30, 1964, I replied to the deputy minister as follows:
Your letter of March 26th dealing with the case of the owner of an insurance and travel agency and resident of the city of Fort William is one which requires further explanation.
This individual was granted landed immigrant status in May 1951. According to your own statement, he was getting along fine. He was a good worker and I have the testimony of the firms he worked for.
In August 1953 he suffered a nervous breakdown, and was admitted to the Ontario Hospital at Port Arthur, Ontario. A few days later he left the hospital, to return for several months.
Because he was an immigrant, without a certificate of citizenship, the case was brought to the attention of the Immigration Department, the officials of which ordered his deportation on the grounds that he had become an inmate of a mental hospital. He appealed the deportation order, which was dismissed. However, as he had been discharged from the hospital and had returned to work, deportation proceedings were suspended.
Since 1954 he repeatedly visited the Immigration Office at Fort William, in an effort to have his landed immigrant status restored to enable him to apply for and obtain Canadian citizenship; this has been denied to him.
In your letter you state that, under the present Immigration Act, there is no provision for removing him from the prohibited classes and, unless legislation is passed to change present regulations, no action can be taken to have his deportation order removed.
In the next paragraph of your letter you state that no unfavourable reports have been received concerning this man and that, in his present circumstances, he may be allowed to remain in this country indefinitely under deferred deportation proceedings.
In the same paragraph you state the Immigration officials will review this matter from time to time, and if any change occurs which would allow for restoration of his status, his case will be considered
What is there to review, may I ask, when the man has been absolutely normal for ten years?
I have spoken personally to the priest whose church he attends regularly. I have questioned people who know him and respect him, none of whom had even the slightest idea that he had been a mental case.
I look upon the disposition of this case by your department as being highly unsatisfactory, and I would ask you to be good enough to have an inquiry made by some competent person, as soon as possible.
On May 7, 1964, I received the following memorandum from the deputy minister:
As the result of your letter of March 30th and our subsequent telephone conversation, I have prepared a full report concerning all the circumstances in the case of the individual who has been allowed to remain in Canada under deferred deportation proceedings since 1954.

First, let me say that my letter of March 26th is factually correct. Under present legislation there is no provision for removing him from the prohibited classes and as his landed immigrant status cannot be restored, it is proposed to allow him to remain indefinitely under deferred deportation proceedings. His file is brought forward and reviewed periodically along with those of a number of other persons whose situation is identical. This review is carried out so that the cases will not be forgotten and to ensure that if it becomes possible to restore landed immigrant status to these persons, it will be done as quickly as possible.
Let me assure you that all concerned are as dissatisfied as you are with the old fashioned provisions of the act pertaining to mental disorders. I would be very pleased if there were some means by which the minister could exercise discretion to 'land' this individual and with this thought in mind, full particulars of the case have been referred to both the departmental legal adviser and the Department of National Health and Welfare for review.
Our legal adviser has expressed the opinion that the deportation order made against him was arrived at in a regular manner, in accord with the requirements of the Immigration Act and there was no error or irregularity in the proceedings that would afford grounds to quash it. When arrived at regularly in this way there is, of course, no discretion in the minister to quash the order-the minister being required in this respect to obey the law as much as other persons. The legal adviser has expressed the opinion that it is not possible to quash the deportation order.
The National Health and Welfare officials have reviewed the file and according to their report, he was treated in the Ontario Hospital, Fort William, on two occasions-from August 18, 1953, until September 8, 1953, and from September 27, 1953 until November 6, 1953. At each admission the diagnosis was the same-catatonic schizophrenia. Catatonic schizophrenia is a psychotic illness.
They state that 'insanity' is a legal, not a medical term. For practical purposes they regard psychotic illness and insanity as synonymous. Consequently, were he now being examined as an immigrant he would be certifiable under Section 5, s.s. (a) (i) of the Immigration Act for previous insanity (catatonic schizophrenia). The accuracy of the diagnosis in relation to the symptoms upon which it was based leaves no room for manoeuvre.
In their report it is explained that when the Immigration Act was framed, insanity was regarded as an incurable illness. It is now known to be temporary in certain cases. This individual, following successful treatment in 1953, has been well for over ten years and they would consider that the risk of recurrence is very small indeed. The certification under Section 5, s.s. (a) (ii) which would be applicable now would be based upon history alone. It is quite possible that his present condition would permit of no certification at all.
However, Section 5, s.s. (a) (ii) refers to immigrants who have been insane at any time. 'Upgrading' would require the 1953 diagnosis to be shown to be wrong and unfortunately, all the evidence in their possession indicates that it was correct.
I realize that this report is rather lengthy and somewhat involved but I do hope that it will convince you that we have not treated him unfairly
March 22, 1968

and that his landed immigrant status is not being restored because the Immigration Act precludes this action.
Now, Mr. Speaker, one can readily understand what prompted me to introduce this bill, which has been on the order paper for over two years and which I hope the house will approve in principle without delay. I wish to express deep appreciation to the minister and his officials for their co-operation and understanding in respect of this vital question. I also express the hope that everyone present will vote for the passage of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, the members of the New Democratic party fully support the amendment brought forward by the hon. member. Possibly the reason he has brought this forward is that, having been born in a European country, I believe Italy, since coming to Canada he has experienced some of these problems at first hand in his area, and therefore has become very sensitve to them. No doubt he is very anxious that these problems be cleared up, not only for the benefit of the people whom he represents but also people all across Canada who are in a similar position.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
If the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) were here, he could cite many examples of the same problem that the hon. member has experienced. He could give in detail the results he has obtained in trying to help these people. I also come from a riding in
Immigration Act
which many immigrants live. In the last ten years in particular a number of Italian, Greek, German and central European immigrants have come into my riding. Some of them have had problems which are quite similar to those cited by the hon. member. It gives me pleasure to rise and support this amendment because I also am sensitive to the problem and should like to see the amendment carried.
I was very glad that the hon. member gave the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) full credit in this respect, because the hon. member knows as well as the rest of us that this minister is a man of great compassion and understanding. I do not doubt that this compassion and understanding derives from his training in the labour movement and experience as a former member of the C.C.F. party and the New Democratic party. I am sure that experience had a great deal of influence on him. We are happy to understand that he supports this amendment.
The provisions of this section were probably drafted at a time when there was not a great deal of immigration to Canada. It was probably passed when we had limited immigration to this country. It may be, therefore, that the problem did not arise with such severity as it does today. If I have any criticism of the section and this amendment it is with regard to the word "insane". Hon. members will notice that the section reads in part, "are insane or, if immigrants, have been insane at any time", and so on. The word "insane" is not generally accepted by Canadians today. It connotes something that we do not really like to think about. We have got rid of the title "insane institutions" and call them mental institutions. I would hope there would be a further amendment to the section and the word "insane" changed to the phrase "mental illness", because what the amendment is aimed at is that if a person suffers from mental illness, and through treatment is cured for at least seven years, this indicates that he should be considered to be a proper applicant for Canadian citizenship. We agree wholeheartedly with this principle and would like not only this amendment to be adopted but a change made in respect of the word "insane".
I notice that the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) seconded the motion. I think he could tell us about this problem in dramatic terms, because he comes from a riding in which many European people live. He has probably had similar experiences with regard

Immigration Act
to the problems of immigrants. I should also like to think we were big enough and possessed enough understanding to make further amendments in order to deal with these problems.
I am sure hon. members have had the following experience. An applicant has applied for immigration to Canada, he and his wife have passed all the necessary tests, but they had one child who was mentally ill. As a result of the child being insane, in the rough words of the section, the applicant has been refused permission to enter Canada. I have heard of devious methods being employed to overcome this difficulty. The father and mother come into this country with the rest of their children and leave in Europe the young-ester who is suffering from a mental illness. Then they get down on their knees and try to persuade the minister that the youngster should be admitted to this country now or at a later time. I should like to think we were big enough that if this type of case arose the youngster could be brought over here, and even if that child were not granted Canadian citizen status the family could live together and the child could be given the treatment and facilities necessary in order to cure the mental illness. He could later be made a Canadian citizen.
These are some of the improvements that we of the New Democratic party would like to see adopted in our immigration laws. As I said, if our main expert on the subject of immigration was in the house, the hon. member for Greenwood, I think he would be able to explain the problems in more detail and more persuasively than I have. We would like to see this amendment adopted, and other changes made to the legislation so that more applicants for immigration to Canada would be accepted.

I think it can be said that these experts in the field of mental problems feel that the existing immigration law is deficient in three respects. First of all it is medically unsound since the mentally ill do, in many cases, recover. Second, it is inflexible and restrictive because in deciding whether to admit these people we should not confine our consideration to their past illness but take into account many other factors, especially the medical opinion and their family circumstances. Third, the existing prohibition is costly to our country because many qualified people who could contribute something to this country are lost to Canada as a result of this absolute prohibition against immigrants who have been mentally ill, even for a short period of time.
I think it can be said that, subject to an amendment which I intend to move in committee at the request of the sponsor, Bill C-30 will meet with the general approval of the medical associations which gave the joint committee the benefit of their views. Certainly the bill would make the present Immigration Act much more flexible. It does recognize that these unfortunate people who have been afflicted with insanity can recover and make a worth-while contribution to the Canadian community. It allows the governor in council to take into account not only the advice of a medical practitioner but the general circumstances of each individual case.
I realize that the Canadian Mental Health Association was critical of a bill similar to Bill C-30 as it was presented to the house originally. I believe the basis for that criticism has for the most part been met by the revision to Bill C-30 made by its sponsor, and which I will be proposing. It is true it does not speak of mental diseases, but it speaks of symptoms of insanity, which is pretty much the same thing.
As members will recall, the government retained Mr. Joseph Sedgwick, Q.C. to report on immigration law. Part II of his report dated January 27, 1966 and later tabled in the house carried a recommendation on the section of the Immigration Act now under discussion. At page 5 he said:
The provisions of the act dealing with "Prohibited Classes" on grounds of health, should, I think, be reviewed, particularly section 5(a) (ii) which bars persons who "are insane or, if immigrants, have been insane at any time".
Many highly desirable immigrants may have had a mental breakdown which resulted in extended treatment, and even confinement in an
Immigration Act
institution. But such persons may, and often do, make a complete recovery, and if they have recovered their past misfortunes should not be, as it now is, an absolute bar to their admission.
I should like for a moment or two to review the law as it presently exists. First of all I will read section 5(a) of the Immigration Act, chapter 325 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, volume 5. It reads as follows:
No person, other than a person referred to in subsection (2) of section 7, shall be admitted to Canada if he is a member of any of the following classes of persons:
(a)	persons who
(i)	are idiots, imbeciles or morons,
(ii)	are insane or, if immigrants, have been insane at any time,
(iii)	have constitutional psychopathic personalities, or
(iv)	if immigrants, are afflicted with epilepsy;
Then section 7 (2) reads as follows:
In addition to the persons described in subsection (1), the following persons may be allowed to enter and remain in Canada as non-immigrants:
(a)	persons authorized by the minister to enter Canada for treatment and care at any health resort, hospital, sanitarium, asylum or other place or institution for their cure and care and, after entering Canada, while they are actually under such treatment and care;
(b)	persons passing in transit through Canada under escort or guard; and
(c)	holders of a permit.
This last subsection takes us to section 8 of the act which reads as follows:
(1)	The minister may issue a written permit authorizing any person to enter Canada or, being in Canada, to remain therein.
(2)	A permit shall be expressed to be in force for a specified period not exceeding twelve months, and during the time that it is in force a permit stays the execution of any deportation order that may have been made against the person concerned.
(3)	The minister may at any time, in writing, extend or cancel a permit.
(4)	The minister may, upon the cancellation or expiration of a permit, make a deportation order respecting the person concerned and such person has no right of appeal from the deportation order and shall be deported as soon as practicable.
(5)	The minister shall submit to parliament within thirty days of the commencement of the first session of parliament in each year a report showing all permits, with particulars thereof, issued during the preceding calendar year.
So we have the situation where wealthy people in Canada can bring in a person who has suffered from a mental illness, temporary or otherwise, and have them hospitalized in Canada under a permit, provided they can make arrangements with the provincial government and can cover the cost which, I understand, is in some cases about $50 a day. Here we have people who in many cases may not recover from their illness, who can come

March 22, 1968
Immigration Act
into Canada-although it is true they may not be able to stay too long-whereas people who have recovered long ago from a temporary mental illness are still barred from coming.
There is a discrimination here, and the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) makes common sense to me and, it appears, does also to all hon. members of the house. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration is fully in favour of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Fort William, which I will be moving at the request of the hon. member. This amendment was drafted after discussion with the minister and the government, and it is one -which is acceptable to the government.
Before I resume my seat perhaps I should advise the house as to the number of permits which have been issued in the last couple of years pertaining to the classes of persons outlined in section 5, and who are permitted to come into Canada under section 8 of the Immigration Act.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In 1966-67 there were respectively 65 and 72 idiots, imbeciles and morons admitted under section 5 (a) (i) which is the subparagraph before the one we are now seeking to have amended. In those years there were 37 and 41 respectively who were insane at some time. In so far as psychopathic personalities are concerned there were 2 and 6 in those years who were admitted. In 1966 there were 72 admitted who were suffering from epilepsy, and 60 in 1967. The total number of persons admitted in these classes was 176 in 1966, and 179 in 1967.

Mr. Chairman, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Spadina appears to be acceptable with one exception. I notice that in (A) he has included the words ''for at least seven years immediately preceding the date of his application for admission he has neither been a patient in any hospital". I am wondering whether the hon. member would agree to qualify that and insert the word "permanent" patient. Some people who have breakdowns do require outpatient treatment even though they are out working in society after treatment for their illness in hospital. In other words, they could be outpatients rather than inpatients.
One would like to think, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member is referring to a permanent patient. There is this limitation of seven years, and it could easily be suggested that a person is a patient if he is receiving outpatient treatment. As you know, when persons recover from an illness they sometimes have a slight relapse. This usually means they have to go back to hospital for a week end or some short period for shock treatment, or some type of treatment, and this would mean that the seven year period would commence from the time they were discharged from hospital. Surely the hon. member for Spadina does not have that in mind.
Patients in hospital beds are usually sent to the hospital by medical doctors. Then after treatment they are discharged. However, sometimes the discharge is conditional upon their attending the outpatient clinic for further treatment. Therefore I would ask the hon. member to consider this change, in the interests of those who may be placed in this position.

Mr. Chairman, might I have a minute or two to consider this. There is some difficulty with the words that follow, "nor suffered any significant recurrence of the symptoms thereof". It might well be that if a person went to hospital as an outpatient and took two shock treatments he would be eliminated under this part in any event.
This question has been well considered by the minister of immigration, and I take it by the justice department, and it seems to me that at this point it would be dangerous to insert a word like "permanent". It would be too all embracing. It may go a little too far, even further than the hon. member for Broadview, who has the best intentions in the matter, would like to go.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about the latter part of paragraph (A), which says "nor suffered any significant recurrence of the symptoms thereof". It is a question of fact. If a person goes to hospital as an outpatient, it might be for treatment that is determined to have no relationship to mental illness. Or it may be for something so insignificant that it would have very little or no bearing on the decision. If it did, then I would think there would be quite an outcry about it.
If we do find, Mr. Chairman, that there are cases arising which give cause for concern, there is always the remedy of making further amendments. However, I submit to the hon. member for Broadview that we would be taking a great step forward if we were to put the bill through as amended at this point. Knowing he is favourable to the amendment I ask him to support it, even though the bill is not as perfect as he might like.

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported and read the third time and passed.
